payload.output: Mitosis is a type of cell division in which a single cell divides to produce two genetically identical daughter cells. The process consists of several phases: prophase, where chromosomes condense; metaphase, where chromosomes line up along the cell's equator; anaphase, where sister chromatids separate and move to opposite poles; and telophase, where new nuclear envelopes form. Cytokinesis then splits the cytoplasm to complete division.
payload.context: Mitosis is a form of cell division that results in two daughter cells, each with the same number and kind of chromosomes as the parent cell. It consists of four main phases: prophase (chromosomes condense and become visible), metaphase (chromosomes align at the metaphase plate), anaphase (sister chromatids are pulled apart to opposite poles), and telophase (nuclear envelopes re-form around each set of chromosomes). Cytokinesis typically follows, dividing the cytoplasm to produce two separate cells.
